evidence.ai_role: A learned gradient-boosted model combines mechanistic and pharmacogenomic features to rank drug dependencies, placing ceralasertib second for held-out MBD4.
evidence.tested: Retrospective GDSC2 cell-line drug-response associations and leave-one-DDR-anchor-out evaluation of a learned drug-prioritization model. The TP53-mutant ceralasertib comparison contains 11 MBD4-loss and 619 wild-type cell lines.
evidence.unknown: The reviewed study does not establish causal MBD4-dependent drug sensitivity or clinical benefit; isogenic perturbation/rescue and prospective clinical evaluation remain outstanding. Existing pharmacogenomic measurements enter model features and do not independently validate its predictions.

source_review.scope: Primary v1 and v2 full-text Methods, pharmacogenomic results, ranker evaluation and limitations; independently retrieved bioRxiv version metadata. Organization field follows the represented v1 affiliations; v2 lists CrisPRO.ai.

summary: A preprint combined the gradient-boosted SL-XGBRanker with retrospective pharmacogenomic analyses to prioritize drug hypotheses for MBD4 loss of function. In existing GDSC2 measurements, TP53-mutant MBD4-loss cell lines were associated with greater ceralasertib sensitivity than wild-type comparators (11 versus 619 lines; reported BH-FDR q=0.036); the ranker placed ceralasertib second when MBD4 was held out during training. The ranking includes pharmacogenomic features from these datasets, so the association is not an independent experimental validation of the model. The small observational cell-line study establishes neither causal synthetic lethality nor clinical benefit; isogenic knockout and rescue experiments remain necessary. The findings appear in the November 12 first public version; a November 20 revision changes author affiliations while retaining them.
title: Learned ranking prioritizes ceralasertib for MBD4-deficient cell lines
